title_en: The Forgotten Godmother of Economic Literature
title_zh: 被遗忘的经济学文学教母
subtitle_zh: 《纽约时报》布鲁塞尔分社社长 Jeanna Smialek 谈玛丽亚·埃奇沃思：这位19世纪的畅销小说家如何把亚当·斯密的经济学讲给大众，又为何从经济思想史中被彻底抹去
description: The Forgotten Godmother of Economic Literature

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios. Podcasts. Radio. News.
turns.zh: 彭博音频工作室（Bloomberg Audio Studios）。播客。广播。新闻。

turns.en: Hello and welcome to another episode of the Oddlots Podcast. I'm Tracey Alloway.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎收听新一期的《Odd Lots》播客。我是崔西·阿洛韦（Tracy Alloway）。

turns.en: And I'm Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: 我是乔·韦森塔尔（Joe Weisenthal）。

turns.en: Joe, something I like to think about is how ideas, specifically economic ideas— go viral, how they get popularized. And so you think about something like the invisible hand.
turns.zh: 乔，我平时很喜欢琢磨一件事：观念——尤其是经济学观念——是怎么走红、怎么被普及开来的。比如说“看不见的手”（the invisible hand）。

turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: A lot of people will recognize that phrase and have a sort of basic understanding of what it means, even if they've never actually read the works of Adam Smith.
turns.zh: 很多人一听到这个说法就能认出来，也大致明白它是什么意思，哪怕他们从来没真正读过亚当·斯密（Adam Smith）的著作。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: I'm actually very fascinated by the concept of pre-internet virality.
turns.zh: 我其实非常着迷于“前互联网时代的爆红”这个概念。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: It's like someone says something online and everyone retweets it. Like, all right, I get how, I get how that works.
turns.zh: 比如说某个人的话在网上发出来，所有人都转发。好吧，这种传播机制我懂。

turns.en: Or says something on a podcast.
turns.zh: 或者说是在播客里讲了什么。

turns.en: Or says something on a podcast, whatever. But like, how did ideas spread back? I mean, especially before electronic media. But they did. I mean, they did spread. You know, I always think about like, it's a little different, but like school children, like rhyming games and stuff like that. And how like all around the world and all around the country, children will be like doing roughly the same, like sort of like games and stuff. Like, how did they, how did it get around so far?
turns.zh: 或者在播客里说了点什么，随便吧。但问题是，过去观念是怎么传播开的？尤其是在电子媒体出现之前。可它们确实传播开了，我是说，真的传播开了。你知道，我总会想到——虽然性质有点不一样——小学生玩的押韵童谣游戏之类的。全世界、全国各地的孩子，玩的游戏大致都差不多。那这些东西到底是怎么传得那么远的？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: It's like, really, I'm fascinated by this question.
turns.zh: 说真的，这个问题让我特别着迷。

turns.en: It's a good question. And before there was social media, before there was podcasts, one of the ways that ideas would get spread around is through fiction, basically, through novels, through stories, as you just pointed out.
turns.zh: 这是个好问题。在社交媒体出现之前、在播客出现之前，观念得以广泛传播的途径之一，基本上就是靠虚构作品——靠小说、靠故事，就像你刚才指出的那样。

turns.en: Right. And it's interesting because we think of ideas, particularly economic ideas, as you said, you referred to the invisible hand. We think of ideas as being like, okay, I'm going to read some ideas. It's going to rationally make sense to me, and then I'll either adopt this idea or I will discard it, et cetera. But a very powerful way of spreading ideas is through things that are fun or things that make us feel good to read, et cetera. And to your point, I think people forget that the transmission of ideas is not just a sort of calculation. It's through art, it's through stories, it's through poetry, it's through music, et cetera. And this almost never gets discussed. In a sort of intellectual context.
turns.zh: 没错。而且有意思的是，我们通常以为观念——尤其是经济学观念，就像你说的，你提到了“看不见的手”——我们以为观念是这样运作的：好，我去读一些观点，它们在理性上说通，然后我要么接受这个观念，要么把它丢掉，诸如此类。但传播观念的一种极其有力的方式，其实是靠那些有趣的、读起来让人愉悦的东西。而且照你的说法，我觉得人们忘了，观念的传递并不只是一种理性算计，它是通过艺术、通过故事、通过诗歌、通过音乐等等来实现的。而在知识界的讨论里，这一点几乎从来没人谈。

turns.en: No, and Adam Smith never wrote a novel to popularize his ideas. But someone who did write about economics through the medium of fiction is going to be our subject for today. We're going to be talking about Maria Edgeworth. who was a very successful novelist in the early 1800s, I guess during the Regency era, who was also very, very involved with shaping the future of economic thought. And she was reading all these people like Adam Smith and actually injecting some of those ideas into her various stories.
turns.zh: 是的，亚当·斯密从没写过小说来推广自己的思想。但确实有一个人用虚构小说这种媒介来写经济学，她就是我们今天要讲的主角。我们要谈的是玛丽亚·埃奇沃思（Maria Edgeworth）。她是19世纪初——我想是摄政时期（Regency era）——一位非常成功的小说家，同时也深度参与了经济思想未来走向的塑造。她读了亚当·斯密这些人的著作，并且真的把其中一些观念注入到她写的各种故事里。

turns.en: Prior to having prepped for this episode, had you heard of her?
turns.zh: 在为这期节目做功课之前，你听说过她吗？

turns.en: No, I had not. Have you?
turns.zh: 没有，我没听说过。你呢？

turns.en: I think this is really interesting.
turns.zh: 我觉得这件事特别有意思。

turns.en: Neither as an economic thinker nor as a novelist, actually.
turns.zh: 说实话，无论是作为经济思想家，还是作为小说家，我都没听说过。

turns.en: And so I'm very intrigued by this.
turns.zh: 所以我对此非常好奇。

turns.en: Yeah. So this is something else that I'm very interested in is like who gets to decide who gets the credit for various economic ideas and which theories we currently view as rational and reasonable. But I know of her now because I read this book. And it's been described as Bridgerton for nerds, which I kind of love because it's a Regency era novelist. And I always thought Bridgerton, like if there's one thing it could use, it's more discussion of agricultural productivity and rent seeking behavior on the part of the wealthy class. So that's what we're going to do today. We're going to talk about Maria Edgeworth, her contribution to economics, and I guess how her ideas, you know, kind of got forgotten in And who gets the credit nowadays?
turns.zh: 嗯。还有一点我也很感兴趣：到底是谁来决定各种经济学观念的功劳该记在谁头上，以及我们今天把哪些理论视为理性、合理。不过我现在知道她了，因为我读了这本书。有人把它形容成“给书呆子看的《布里奇顿》（Bridgerton）”，这个说法我还挺喜欢的，因为主角就是摄政时期的小说家。我一直觉得，《布里奇顿》要是能多加点东西，那就该多谈谈农业生产率，以及有闲阶级的寻租（rent seeking）行为。所以我们今天要做的就是这个：谈谈玛丽亚·埃奇沃思、她对经济学的贡献，以及她的思想是怎么被遗忘的，还有如今这些功劳都被记在了谁头上。

turns.en: I'm excited about this one.
turns.zh: 这期我很期待。

turns.en: It's a really good book. And I'm very happy to say we have the perfect guest to discuss it. We're going to be speaking to the author, Gina Smilak. She is... A former colleague of ours at Bloomberg, now bureau chief, Brussels bureau chief over at the New York Times.
turns.zh: 这是本非常好的书。而且我很高兴地说，我们请到了讨论它的完美嘉宾。我们将和作者吉安娜·斯米亚莱克（Jeanna Smialek）对话。她……曾是我们彭博的同事，现在是《纽约时报》的布鲁塞尔分社社长。

turns.en: Previously seen in many Fed press conferences.
turns.zh: 以前在很多美联储新闻发布会上都见过她。

turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: Asking questions in a previous version.
turns.zh: 在她上一份工作里，提问的——

turns.en: Of her job. That's exactly right. And the book is The Invisible Hand of Maria Edgeworth, How a 19th Century Novelist Taught the World Everything. economics. So Gina, welcome back to the show.
turns.zh: ——就是她。完全没错。这本书叫《玛丽亚·埃奇沃思的看不见的手：一位19世纪小说家如何教会全世界经济学》（The Invisible Hand of Maria Edgeworth: How a Nineteenth-Century Novelist Taught the World Economics）。那么，吉安娜，欢迎回到我们的节目。

turns.en: Thank you for having me. I'm excited to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们邀请我。很高兴来到这里。

turns.en: So how did you discover Maria Edgeworth? Because as Joe and I were saying prior to the publication of your book, I had never heard of her either in an economics or a literary context.
turns.zh: 那你是怎么发现玛丽亚·埃奇沃思这个人的？因为就像乔和我刚才说的，在你这本书出版之前，无论在经济学语境还是文学语境里，我都没听说过她。

turns.en: So I was, it was about a decade ago. I was working here actually, and I was covering the Federal Reserve and I was relatively new on the Fed beat, trying to learn as much as I could about the ideas I was covering. I didn't have an economics degree at the time. And so I just thought that I needed a little bit more background than I had. And so I was reading a lot of economic history and I read Robert Hillbronner's, The Worldly Philosophers, Seminal History of the Field. And, you know, that book is excellent. It's a fun read, but it's also like, Adam, Bob, John, Mark, you know, you move through history and it's a very male-dominated industry. But he has this little aside that Ricardo, David Ricardo, obviously one of the most famous economists of all of history, was really good friends with this woman named Mariah Edgeworth, called Mariah at the time, called Maria today. And she was probably the first woman to think about economics. And that's the extent of the aside. It's only in some editions of Hale Bronner. So people who have read the book may not even recognize that because he's only got it in the later editions. And it really struck me that I had never heard of this lady. And then I, of course, I Googled her and discovered that she had been outselling Jane Austen in her day and age, which was extremely surprising to me. And so I just went down a rabbit hole and here we are.
turns.zh: 事情大概是十年前。当时我其实就在这儿（彭博）工作，报道美联储，而且我做美联储这条线还相对不久，正在拼命学习我所报道的这些思想。我那时候没有经济学学位，所以觉得自己需要比现有水平更多的背景知识。于是我就大量阅读经济史，读了罗伯特·海尔布罗纳（Robert Heilbroner）的《世俗哲学家》（The Worldly Philosophers）——这个领域的开创性史书。那本书非常出色，读起来很有意思，但它也是“亚当、鲍勃、约翰、马克”这么一路走完历史，是个男性主导得厉害的行业。不过书里有一小段插叙，说李嘉图——大卫·李嘉图（David Ricardo），显然是史上最著名的经济学家之一——和一位名叫玛丽亚·埃奇沃思的女士是挚友，当时人们叫她 Mariah，今天叫 Maria。她可能是第一位思考经济学的女性。这段插叙就这么长，而且只出现在海尔布罗纳这本书的某些版本里。所以读过这本书的人可能根本没注意到，因为只有后来的版本才有。让我深受触动的是，我从没听说过这位女士。然后我当然就去谷歌搜了她，发现她在那个年代的书卖得比简·奥斯汀（Jane Austen）还多，这让我极为惊讶。于是我就一路钻进了这个兔子洞，然后就有了今天。

turns.en: Should we call her Maria or Mariah then?
turns.zh: 那我们该叫她 Maria 还是 Mariah 呢？

turns.en: In the sort of modern era, people usually call her Maria. She's still well-read in Ireland, actually, and they call her Maria.
turns.zh: 在现代，人们通常叫她 Maria。其实在爱尔兰她的作品仍然有很多人读，那儿的人也叫她 Maria。

turns.en: That's actually interesting that in her day she outsold Jane Austen because that raises a second question sort of related to what you're talking about. So, like, who we're reading today may not have any correlation to people who people were reading back then. It's very hard to know, like, who will actually be durable, and sometimes people get rediscovered. Can you explain that? Like, why, if she was outselling Jane Austen in her day, does everyone read Jane Austen and not Maria?
turns.zh: 她在自己那个年代卖得比简·奥斯汀还好，这其实很有意思，因为它引出了第二个问题，和你刚才讲的有点相关。也就是说，我们今天在读谁，可能和当时人们在读谁完全没有关联。很难知道谁能真正经久不衰，而且有些人后来会被重新发掘。你能解释一下吗？既然她当年的销量超过了简·奥斯汀，为什么现在人人都读简·奥斯汀，却没人读玛丽亚？

turns.en: Yeah, so I actually think this is really fascinating because I think two things are true. Sometimes people get forgotten, and she got forgotten in an almost surprising way. So she was extremely famous in her day. Lord Byron once said that she had replaced him as the lion of the season, and he was extremely.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得这件事真的很迷人，因为我认为有两件事同时成立。有时候人会被遗忘，而她被遗忘的方式几乎到了令人吃惊的地步。她在自己那个年代极其出名。拜伦勋爵（Lord Byron）曾经说过，她已经取代他成了当季最耀眼的明星（the lion of the season），而他对此极度——

turns.en: Jealous of this. Actually, it's very funny.
turns.zh: ——嫉妒。这事其实非常好笑。

turns.en: He's got a whole little sequence in his letters where he's being jealous of her. She was read by the royals. She was, you know, across the British Empire. The Americans were really excited about her writing. And so she was incredibly famous.
turns.zh: 他的书信里有一整段都是在吃她的醋。王室在读她的作品，整个大英帝国都在读。美国人对她的写作也非常兴奋。所以她当时红得不得了。

turns.en: She got forgotten.
turns.zh: 然后她就被遗忘了。

turns.en: And I think that a huge part of that is actually that she was putting a lot of pedagogical material in her novels. She took her writing very seriously. She saw it as a way to communicate ideas. And you get into sort of the Jane Austen era. So Maria is really active. Maria is really active from 1795. through sort of 1815 is sort of her heyday. Jane Austen's slightly later. She's sort of like the early 1800s. And so you get into the Jane Austen era and things become a lot more naturalistic. The storytelling is less pedagogical. It's less like hit you over the head with some ideas. And so that is part of why she gets forgotten. I think that actually, ironically, the economics that she's including in her novels is part of her problem. And so I think there's sort of an irony there.
turns.zh: 我觉得其中很大一个原因，其实是她在小说里塞进了大量说教性的内容。她非常认真地对待自己的写作，把它当作传递观念的一种手段。然后就进入了简·奥斯汀的时代。玛丽亚真正活跃的时间是从1795年开始，到1815年前后是她的鼎盛期。简·奥斯汀稍晚一些，大概是19世纪初。到了简·奥斯汀的时代，作品变得自然主义得多了，叙事的说教味淡了，不再像那样把某些观念硬敲进你脑子里。这就是她被遗忘的部分原因。而且我认为，很讽刺的是，她写进小说里的经济学恰恰是她的问题所在。所以这里面有种反讽。

turns.en: Well, OK, so talk to us about when we say that she tried to illustrate economic ideas through her writings, what would be an example of that? And I have to say, I read your book. I did not read. I didn't have time to read one of Edgeworth's actual books. I did read a short story for children called The Cherry Orchard, where she kind of gets into the division of labor. It was a very boring story, I got to say, and to your point, very much sort of hitting you over the head with its message. But like what did her writing actually look like and how did she deal with economics?
turns.zh: 好，那跟我们说说，当我们讲她试图通过写作来阐释经济学观念时，具体有什么例子？我得说，我读了你的书，但我没来得及读埃奇沃思本人的作品。我确实读了一篇叫《樱桃园》（The Cherry Orchard）的儿童短篇，她在里面讲到了分工（division of labor）。说实话，那是个很无聊的故事，而且正如你说的，非常直白地把它的训诫往你脑子里砸。那么她的写作实际是什么样子，她又是怎么处理经济学的？

turns.en: Yeah. So a bunch of her. So she was prolific. She wrote a lot. Not all of her work deals with economics, but quite a big portion of her catalog does. She does it differently for different audiences.
turns.zh: 嗯。她的作品……她很多产，写了大量东西。不是所有作品都涉及经济学，但她作品目录里相当大一部分是涉及的。而且面对不同读者群，她的写法也不一样。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: So the children's audience, she is writing very much to be read in the nursery as sort of a like early learning when you're learning how to read kind of text. And so it's very simplistic. She has a slightly more complex version of economics for adults and particularly for elite adults. So an example of that is her novel On We, which is one of her more famous novels at the time. And in my opinion, the one that still scans the best in modern reading. So if listeners want to start with a Mariah Edgeworth book, I would recommend On We. It's a fun book. But that one has a very sophisticated take on economics.
turns.zh: 面向儿童读者时，她写的东西基本上是为了在育儿室里朗读，属于孩子刚学认字时的启蒙读物，所以非常浅显。而面向成人，尤其是精英阶层的成人，她提供的是稍复杂一些版本的经济学。一个例子就是她的小说《倦怠》（Ennui），这是她当时比较有名的小说之一，而且在我看来，也是今天读起来依然最站得住脚的一部。所以如果听众想从玛丽亚·埃奇沃思的作品入手，我会推荐《Ennui》。这本书很好读，但它对经济学的处理是非常精深的。

turns.en: It's extensive.
turns.zh: 分量很足。

turns.en: There's essentially a chapter and a half that's just solely dedicated to economics. And then the rest of the book has it kind of woven in and out throughout. And she also at times just basically does essays. So she's got a book called Letters for Literary Ladies, which is, you know, it's framed as fiction. It's a bunch of letters in between various people discussing whether women should be in the labor market. It's very much building on Adam Smith. She's writing just after Adam Smith. This is her first book. And so it's very much sort of an argument, but she's making it in a fictional format because she's a woman and she is not allowed to publish academic papers. So I think it really varies between extremely simplistic and very sophisticated.
turns.zh: 书里基本上有一章半完全是专门讲经济学的，剩下的部分则把经济学时不时地穿插编织进去。她有时候干脆就是写论文。比如她有一本书叫《致文学女士的信》（Letters for Literary Ladies），它被包装成虚构作品，是一堆不同人之间的书信，讨论女性是否应该进入劳动力市场。它非常直接地承接亚当·斯密——她写作的时间就紧随斯密之后，这是她的第一本书。所以它其实很像一个论辩，但她用虚构的形式来展开，因为她是女性，不被允许发表学术论文。所以我觉得她的作品跨度真的很大，从极其浅显到非常精深都有。

turns.en: Do you like her books?
turns.zh: 你喜欢她的书吗？

turns.en: I like some of them. Some of them are slog because she's writing at a time when books are very long, when books are very dry sometimes. I think it's important context for readers to know that or listeners to know that. at the time that she is writing, the novel is still in its formation. It has not solidified into the format that we know today. She actually helps it to do that, as do most of her contemporaries. And so they're not really sure what they're doing. It's an era of experimentation. And so you see a lot of her novels really ranging with that experimentation. Like as people are trying to figure out what these should look like, she's changing her style. And I think she also is making them slightly boring and making them slightly wonky in the service of making them seem serious. So at the time, novels are mostly written by women for women. They're seen as light and stupid and trivial. And so she's trying to say, like, no, these are not light and stupid and trivial. There's a way to take these seriously. She actually calls her novels moral tales, somewhat hilariously, because she doesn't want them to get, like, stained by the label of novel.
turns.zh: 我喜欢其中一些。有些读起来很费劲，因为她写作的那个年代，书都很长，有时候也很枯燥。我觉得读者或听众需要了解的一个重要背景是：在她写作的时候，小说这种体裁还在形成之中，还没有定型为我们今天熟悉的样子。她其实帮助了它完成这个定型，她的大多数同代人也是如此。所以他们其实并不太确定自己在做什么，那是一个实验的时代。你会看到她很多小说都在这种实验中四处摆动——人们在摸索小说该是什么样子，她也在不断改变自己的风格。而且我觉得，为了让作品显得严肃，她还刻意把它们写得稍微无聊一点、稍微学究气一点。因为在那个时代，小说大多是女性写给女性看的，被视为轻浮、愚蠢、琐碎。所以她想说的是：不，这些东西并不轻浮愚蠢琐碎，是有办法认真对待它们的。她甚至把自己的小说叫作“道德故事”（moral tales），有点好笑，因为她不想让作品被“小说”这个标签玷污。

turns.en: But they're very clearly novels. Oh, interesting.
turns.zh: 但它们明明就是小说啊。哦，有意思。

turns.en: You know, it's funny. Have you heard of Russell Roberts' The Invisible Heart and Economic Romance? Have you heard of this book? No. Yeah, so Russell Roberts is an economist. It was sort of popular in the early 2000s. there was a lot of, you know, like sort of like Koch brothers, George Mason University-esque money that was put forth towards let's create art that like smuggles in, basically like free market, libertarian market ideas. So like people like wrote econ novels, et cetera. And I'm sort of curious, like, cause you said trying to hit people over the head a little bit, maybe that's why they're not read as much. Like, I'm curious how it compares to like the other efforts over the years. Like, Let's teach children the importance of free enterprise by writing. Did she have an ideology? Was there an overarching lesson?
turns.zh: 你知道吗，挺有意思的。你听说过拉塞尔·罗伯茨（Russell Roberts）的《看不见的心：一个经济学爱情故事》（The Invisible Heart: An Economic Romance）吗？你听说过这本书吗？没有？是这样，罗伯茨是位经济学家。21世纪初这类东西挺流行的，当时有很多——你懂的——科赫兄弟（Koch brothers）、乔治梅森大学（George Mason University）那种风格的资金，投入到“让我们来创作一些艺术品，把自由市场、自由意志主义的市场观念偷偷夹带进去”这件事上。所以有人写经济学小说等等。我就有点好奇，因为你刚才说她有点想把观念硬敲进读者脑子里，也许这就是她的书现在没那么多人读的原因。我好奇的是，跟这些年来其他类似的努力相比，她怎么样？比如“让我们通过写作教孩子自由企业制度的重要性”。她有一套意识形态吗？有没有一个统领性的教训？

turns.en: When you said Koch brothers and romantic economic literature, I thought you were going to go in a very different direction. But the Koch with a K brothers.
turns.zh: 你刚说科赫兄弟和“经济学罗曼史”的时候，我以为你要往一个完全不同的方向讲。不过就是拼作 K 的那个科赫兄弟。

turns.en: Oh, yes.
turns.zh: 哦，是的。

turns.en: K-O-C-H.
turns.zh: K-O-C-H。

turns.en: Yeah. I think the important distinction here and the context that's really important is she is writing in sort of 1795, sort of her start date. So Adam Smith has just written The Wealth of Nations in 1776. She's generation one. Like she's the first set of people starting to understand economic ideas. And so I think because I think, you know, most people date the start of modern economics to 1776 and The Wealth of Nations. And her dad is friends with the crowd that Smith working in. He doesn't know Smith personally, but he knows all of Smith's best friends. And so she's got a really front row seat as early economics is being developed. And she's doing her best to popularize this set of ideas that nobody knows yet. So I think while sort of modern takes on this are more like, believe my ideology, she is more like, there's a new way of thinking about the world in town.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得这里重要的区别、以及真正关键的背景是：她开始写作大约在1795年，那是她的起点。而亚当·斯密刚刚在1776年写出《国富论》（The Wealth of Nations）。她属于第一代，是最早开始理解经济学观念的那批人之一。我想，大多数人会把现代经济学的起点定在1776年和《国富论》。她父亲和斯密所处的那个圈子是朋友——他不认识斯密本人，但他认识斯密所有最好的朋友。所以在早期经济学被创立出来的过程中，她坐在真正的前排位置。她在尽最大努力去普及这套还没有人了解的观念。所以我认为，现代那类做法更像是“请相信我的意识形态”，而她更像是“镇上刚来了一种理解世界的新方式”。

turns.en: Yeah, I see.
turns.zh: 嗯，我明白了。

turns.en: Why don't you take a look at this? And she thinks she, I think, almost uniquely at the time when she's starting to write, thinks that these ideas need to be translated for normal people. So she's writing just in the wake of the French Revolution. People have democratic power that they hadn't necessarily had before. The American Revolution has just happened as well. Sort of the whole world is in the state of flux and change. The Industrial Revolution is is very much in the sights. It's not really fully in form yet, but it's clear that it's coming and the elites understand that. And so she's really thinking about like a new world is dawning. How do we educate people to be ready for it? And she thinks that economic education is an important part of that. And so I think that a lot of her ideology is really surrounding how do we apply the ideas in the wealth of nations in broader ways? And a lot of her early contributions are basically taking the ideas that she finds in the wealth of nations and making them more for the real world.
turns.zh: 你不妨看看这个。而且我认为，在她刚开始写作的那个时代，她几乎是独一无二地认为，这些观念需要被“翻译”给普通人。她写作的时点正好在法国大革命之后，人们获得了此前未必拥有过的民主权力；美国革命也刚刚发生；整个世界处于流动和变化之中。工业革命已经近在眼前，虽然还没有完全成形，但很明显它要来了，而精英阶层也明白这一点。所以她真正在思考的是：一个新世界正在破晓，我们该如何教育人们去迎接它？她认为经济教育是其中很重要的一部分。所以我觉得，她的意识形态很大程度上是围绕着“我们如何把《国富论》里的观念应用到更宽广的领域”，而她早期的很多贡献，基本上就是把她从《国富论》里读到的观念，改造成更适合现实世界的东西。

turns.en: Yeah. So give us maybe a concrete example. So when I initially looked her up as I was reading this book, the book that came up first was Castle Rackrent, which it turns out is directly borrowed from the Adam Smith text, this idea of rack rent. What were the Smithian, Smithsonian, I don't know.
turns.zh: 嗯。那给我们举个具体的例子吧。我读这本书的时候最初去查她，最先跳出来的作品是《拉克伦特城堡》（Castle Rackrent），结果发现“rack rent”（苛租）这个概念是直接从亚当·斯密的文本里借来的。那些斯密式的——Smithian 还是 Smithsonian，我也搞不清——

turns.en: Smithian.
turns.zh: Smithian。

turns.en: Smith-esque ideas that were embedded in that book.
turns.zh: 就是那些嵌在这本书里的斯密式观念。

turns.en: Fun fact, it's Smithian. This is actually a word that exists. I did not know this prior to researching this book. But yes, so she writes Rack Rent, which is literally the name of it is pulled straight from Smith. He talks about racked rent, which is a rent that's too high to allow the renter to productively make a profit. And so she pulls the title directly from Adam Smith. The book, this was actually the first Maria Edgeworth book that I personally read. And it is just like a regurgitation of the wealth of nations in large part. And there's actually a lot of, literary historian work that sort of analyzes the ways in which this pulls directly from Smith. So this is not an unknown fact. I am not the first person to observe this. But she pulls very directly from Smith. She talks about a lot of ideas that he talks about in The Wealth of Nations, but applies them to Irish estate owning. So she is Anglo-Irish. She's an English elite who owns an estate in Ireland. Obviously, this becomes much more problematic throughout her life. But when she's young, this is, though, basically the way that Ireland is run. And she's talking about how you can be a landlord in sort of a more moral and productive way, like how this old system can fit into our new capitalistic system. And so so much of what she talks about in Rack Rent is where do you set rents? How do you pay wages? How do you incentivize workers to be more productive? And how do you not squander your resources in a way that sort of runs your estate into the ground? And so she's really taking the stuff that Adam Smith put out very abstractly, simplifying it and applying it to the real world.
turns.zh: 趣闻一则：正确的词就是 Smithian，这确实是个真实存在的词。我在为这本书做研究之前也不知道。是的，她写了《Rack Rent》，书名本身就是直接从斯密那里拿来的。斯密谈到 rack rent，指的是一种高到让佃户无法有生产力地赚到利润的地租。所以她的书名直接取自亚当·斯密。这本书其实是我个人读的第一本玛丽亚·埃奇沃思，它在很大程度上就是《国富论》的一次复述。而且有相当多文学史方面的研究，分析了这本书在哪些方面直接取自斯密。所以这并不是什么无人知晓的事实，我不是第一个观察到这一点的人。但她确实非常直接地取自斯密。她谈了很多斯密在《国富论》里谈过的观念，只不过把它们应用到了爱尔兰的地产经营上。她是盎格鲁-爱尔兰人（Anglo-Irish），属于在爱尔兰拥有庄园的英格兰精英阶层。显然，这一点在她一生中后来变得问题重重。但在她年轻的时候，这基本上就是爱尔兰的运作方式。她谈的是：你怎样才能做一个更有道德、更有生产力的地主，这套旧制度如何能嵌入我们新的资本主义体系。所以在《Rack Rent》里，她谈的很多东西是：地租该定在什么水平？工资该怎么发？怎样激励工人更有生产力？怎样才不会挥霍资源、把自己的庄园搞垮？所以她真的是把亚当·斯密非常抽象地提出的东西，加以简化并应用到现实世界中。

turns.en: And these are all ideas that still apply to today. Joe, you and I, we both live in New York, and I know we've walked down streets where you have shop faces that have been empty for years and years and years. And you go like, well, why doesn't the landlord just lower the rent and rent it out to someone rather than keeping it empty?
turns.zh: 而这些观念放到今天依然适用。乔，你和我都住在纽约，我知道我们都走过那样的街道，沿街店面空了好多年好多年。你就会想：房东为什么不干脆把租金降下来租给别人，而要让它一直空着？

turns.en: I've asked this question a bunch of times. I'm never satisfied by the answer. Everyone is like, oh, it's just like banks and taxes. Valuations. Valuations. And like, I've never understood this, so I'm still curious. So thinking about economics today, it's just like, especially academic, academic economics specifically, like you might as well in some cases like be reading geometry or math or something like that. There's a lot of equations, et cetera. There's a lot of, I don't, you know, I'm more sympathetic to them than I used to be, but seeming disconnect from like anything else. in the real world, et cetera. You know, especially you read a lot of old economics and it's like people maybe not literally writing novels, though in this case it was, but like sort of stories. And, you know, I think, what did they used to call economics before it was economics?
turns.zh: 这个问题我问过很多次，但从来没有对答案满意过。大家都说：哦，就是银行和税务的问题。估值。估值。可我一直没弄明白，所以我到现在还好奇。所以想想今天的经济学——尤其是学术经济学——有些情况下你还不如说自己在读几何或者数学之类的。里面有大量方程等等。还有很多……我不知道该怎么说，我现在比过去更能体谅他们了，但看起来和现实世界里的任何东西都是脱节的。你知道，尤其是你去读很多早期的经济学著作，那些人也许不是真的在写小说——虽然在这个案例里确实是——但他们在写类似故事的东西。所以我想，经济学在成为“经济学”之前，以前是被叫作什么来着？

turns.en: It was like- Political economy.
turns.zh: 它当时叫——政治经济学（political economy）。

turns.en: Political economy. Like this sort of like telling stories and stuff like that. When did that die off? When was the end of economics taught as a sort of like almost like a moral instruction in a way.
turns.zh: 政治经济学。就是那种讲故事之类的东西。它什么时候消亡的？经济学作为一种近乎道德训导的方式来教授，是什么时候结束的？

turns.en: So this is a fun plot twist that I'm kind of going to give away because it's an important part of the book, actually. But her nephew is a big part of this transition, actually. Yeah, so Mariah Edgeworth's nephew is F.Y. Edgeworth, who your listeners may be familiar with because if they took Econ 101 and they studied the Edgeworth box, so the sort of four-way trade-off that you get in Econ 101, that is her nephew who came up with that idea. And so a lot of microeconomics that we still learn today actually is based on the ideas of Edgeworth.
turns.zh: 这其实是一个有趣的剧情反转，我打算剧透一下，因为它确实是这本书里很重要的一部分。她的侄子在这场转变中占了很大分量。是的，玛丽亚·埃奇沃思的侄子是 F. Y. 埃奇沃思（Francis Ysidro Edgeworth），听众可能对他有印象，因为如果他们上过经济学入门课、学过埃奇沃思盒状图（Edgeworth box）——就是入门课里那种四方权衡的图——那个概念就是她侄子提出来的。所以我们今天仍在学的很多微观经济学，其实都建立在埃奇沃思的思想之上。

turns.en: And it's really the.
turns.zh: 而且真正把

turns.en: Application of utility to economics that takes it from the realm of philosophy to the realm of sort of math and physics. Okay. So there's, there's what some people will, some economic historians will call physics jealousy that sort of springs up in the mid 1800s where economists are sort of.
turns.zh: 效用（utility）概念引入经济学这一步，才把它从哲学的领域带进了数学与物理的领域。好。那么，有些经济史学家会把这称为19世纪中叶兴起的“物理学嫉妒”（physics jealousy），在那时候，经济学家们有点……

turns.en: They want to be a science, right? Yeah.
turns.zh: 他们想成为一门科学，对吧？嗯。

turns.en: They're looking around and they're like, oh, people are taking these scientists seriously. And so they really want to become more serious. They want to be involved at universities. At the time, there are very few economists working out of universities. Thomas Malthus is the first sort of academic economist, but it's a relatively rare posting. There aren't a lot of them at the time. And so they start, they form this thing called the Political Economy Club. They don't invite any of the women working in economics at the time to the Political Economy Club. And they start working really hard to sort of make economics a little bit mathier. Ricardo had kind of started with this abstraction, but it's really the marginalists. So the group of people who take utility theory and apply it to economics, who kind of successfully make this transition happen because they successfully sort of write down models and say that these models describe the world. And so you see the sort of early marginalists, including Edgeworth, but it's sort of the entire crowd of people working on these issues throughout the 1850s, transition this into a very academic pursuit.
turns.zh: 他们四下看看，然后想：哦，人们很认真地在对待这些科学家。所以他们真的很想变得更严肃，想进入大学。在当时，很少有经济学家是在大学里工作的。托马斯·马尔萨斯（Thomas Malthus）算是第一位学院派经济学家，但那还是相当罕见的职位，当时这样的人不多。于是他们成立了一个叫“政治经济学俱乐部”（Political Economy Club）的组织。他们没有邀请当时任何一位从事经济学的女性加入这个俱乐部。然后他们开始非常努力地让经济学变得更数学化一点。李嘉图已经在抽象化方面开了个头，但真正完成这个转变的是边际主义者（marginalists）——也就是那群把效用理论应用到经济学上的人，因为他们成功地写出了模型，并宣称这些模型描述了世界。所以你会看到早期边际主义者，包括埃奇沃思，但其实是一整个在整个19世纪50年代研究这些问题的群体，把经济学转变成了非常学院化的追求。

turns.en: Why were they called the marginalists?
turns.zh: 他们为什么被叫作边际主义者？

turns.en: Because they were.
turns.zh: 因为他们研究的是

turns.en: Working with marginal utility. So utility was originally a philosophical idea.
turns.zh: 边际效用（marginal utility）。所以，效用最初是一个哲学概念。

turns.en: Yeah, right.
turns.zh: 嗯，对。

turns.en: Utilitarian, Jeremy Bentham, all those guys.
turns.zh: 功利主义，杰里米·边沁（Jeremy Bentham），那帮人。

turns.en: Exactly. Exactly.
turns.zh: 正是，正是。

turns.en: And actually, very interestingly, Mariah Edgeworth was extremely interested in utilitarians and was friends with a lot of them. And so she actually– her only sort of known academic work that kind of touches on an economic issue– was an anonymous essay that we only know exists because she had some surviving letters that sort of got through that describe it. She was very set on this essay saying secret, not being attributed to her. But in it, she reviews a translation of Bentham. And in doing so, translates it back. The translation of Bentham is in French. She translates it back into English and simplifies Bentham for the average reader. So she was very interested in utility theory. There's some academic research suggesting that the utilitarian ideas that her nephew came up with probably actually originated with her. And so, yes, so this transition happens. She's kind of on the leading edge of it probably. But what we know for sure is that by sort of the mid-1800s, the political is dropped from political economy. It becomes economics with Alfred Marshall's seminal textbook. And it really becomes an academic sort of, you know, at university pursuit from there.
turns.zh: 而且非常有意思的是，玛丽亚·埃奇沃思对功利主义者极感兴趣，和其中很多人都是朋友。她唯一一部算得上触及经济学问题的学术作品，其实是一篇匿名文章，我们今天之所以知道它存在，只是因为有一些留存下来的书信描述了它。她非常坚持这篇文章要保密、不署名给她。但在这篇文章里，她评述了一个边沁的译本，并在此过程中把它又译了回来。那个边沁译本是法文的，她把它重新译回英文，并为普通读者简化了边沁。所以她对效用理论非常感兴趣。有一些学术研究表明，她侄子提出的那些功利主义观念，很可能其实源自她本人。所以，是的，这场转变就这样发生了，她大概就处在这场转变的最前沿。但我们能确定的是，到了19世纪中叶前后，“政治经济学”里的“政治”被去掉了，随着阿尔弗雷德·马歇尔（Alfred Marshall）那本开创性的教科书，它变成了“经济学”（economics），从那以后就真的成了一种学院里的、大学里的学术追求。

turns.en: This is sort of, I guess, a cultural or historical question, but, you know, why didn't she ever publish under a male pen name? Because it's not like it was unheard of. Maybe later in the 1800s, the Bronte sisters published under a male pseudonym. Her father was an economist. I guess she had her nephew who became an economist as well. Why did she choose to publish under her own name?
turns.zh: 这大概算是个文化或历史问题，但她为什么从来没有用男性笔名发表作品？因为那也不是什么闻所未闻的事。也许到19世纪后期，勃朗特姐妹（Brontë sisters）就是用男性笔名发表的。她父亲是经济学家，我想她侄子后来也成了经济学家。她为什么选择用自己的名字发表？

turns.en: So I think there are a couple of reasons. One is that she's writing fiction, and so it's acceptable for women to do that. And at the time, there were several women publishing under their own name. Frances Burney is writing simultaneously to her. This is a fairly vibrant era for female novelists. It's just after the French Revolution. The full backlash to women being active in sort of the intellectual sphere has not started yet. And so there are other women publishing under their own names. It's fairly common for women at this time to publish anonymously first. It's fairly common, actually, for everybody to publish anonymously first. And she does publish anonymously at first. But she becomes so incredibly famous that people start taking credit for her work. And she really does not love that. So when she writes Rack Rent, at least, I mean, there's very little historical corroboration of this, but her stepmother says that when she writes Rack Rent, they find out that there's a man in England who has produced a, like, pretend manuscript trying to claim that he had written Castle Rackrent because it was, you know, the premier bestseller of the age. And so he wanted to take credit for it. And so after that point, it's anonymous at that point. After that point, she always publishes under her own name. So I think it was really a part of it was about taking claim to her own authorship. But like I said, when she wrote anything more heavily economic, she would often either publish it anonymously in the case of this essay we know about, Or she would get a male colleague or a male relative to write it and publish it under their name. So some of her sort of most academic writing, for example, there's a draft essay on education at Oxford that never got published but was intended for publication. It would have been published under her father's name. She was never intending to publish it under her own name. It's written from his perspective. It is written in her hand with his notes. And just based on his notes, it seems very clear that a lot of the ideas are actually her and not him. But so she really sort of did take on the guise of men, but she took on the guise of real men.
turns.zh: 我觉得有几个原因。一个是她写的是虚构作品，而女性写虚构作品是可以被接受的。而且在当时，已经有好几位女性用真名发表作品了。范妮·伯尼（Frances Burney）和她同时在写作。对女性小说家来说，那是一个相当活跃的时代。那正好是法国大革命之后，对女性活跃于知识界的全面反弹还没有开始。所以还有其他女性在用真名发表作品。在那个时代，女性先匿名发表是相当常见的，其实所有人都先匿名发表都很常见。她一开始也确实是匿名发表的。但她变得极其有名，以至于开始有人冒领她的作品，而她对此非常不喜欢。所以她写《Rack Rent》的时候——我是说，关于这一点几乎没有多少史料佐证——但她的继母说，当时他们发现英格兰有个男人搞出了一份假手稿，声称《拉克伦特城堡》是他写的，因为那是那个时代头号畅销书，所以他想把功劳据为己有。而那之后……当时还是匿名出版的，那之后她就一直用真名发表。所以我觉得，其中一部分原因确实是要主张自己的作者身份。但就像我说的，凡是她写得经济学色彩更重的东西，她往往要么匿名发表——比如我们知道的那篇文章——要么就让一位男性同事或男性亲属来写、用他们的名字发表。所以她那些最学术的写作，比如有一篇关于牛津教育的文章草稿，从未发表，但本来是打算发表的，它本来会以她父亲的名义出版。她从没打算用自己的名字发表，那是从他的视角写的，用她的笔迹写成，上面有他的批注。而且仅从他的批注来看就很清楚，其中很多观念其实是她的，不是他的。所以她确实借用了男性的外壳，只不过借用的是真实存在的男性。

turns.en: She just wrote under other people's names. Can I ask about the potato correspondence? Oh, yes. So you mentioned she was friends with Ricardo earlier, and there's a chapter in the book where they basically go back and forth about potatoes in Ireland and the risks that growing lots of potatoes may or may not cause.
turns.zh: 她就是用别人的名字来写。我能问问那段“土豆通信”吗？哦，当然。你刚才提到她和李嘉图是朋友，书里有一章讲他们基本上就是在来回通信，讨论爱尔兰的土豆，以及大量种植土豆可能带来或者未必带来的风险。

turns.en: Yes. I think this is probably one of the more interesting chapters of her life, particularly to anyone interested in sort of the formation of economic ideas. She became very good friends with both Thomas Malthus and David Ricardo during her time. She used to visit London quite a lot. She had a little bit of a socialite sort.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得这可能是她一生中比较有意思的一段，尤其对任何关注经济学观念如何形成的人来说。她在那个时期和托马斯·马尔萨斯、大卫·李嘉图都成了很好的朋友。她以前经常去伦敦，身上有那么一点社交名媛的

turns.en: Of aspect to her.
turns.zh: ——那种气质。

turns.en: And she was friends with both of them. And after she became friends with Ricardo, they started a very sort of aggressive letter writing campaign to each other in which they were like very friendly, but literally always disagreeing. And so they had a very active debate about economics going on. And the question that they most you know, centrally debated was whether it was okay for Ireland to exclusively specialize in potatoes. Historians read these letters multiple ways, and I think it's very difficult to know for sure what her goals were. But basically, Maria Maria writes to Ricardo and says, I think that we should totally specialize in potatoes. Like I think Ireland should just go all in on the potato, trade for everything else.
turns.zh: 她和他们两位都是朋友。她和李嘉图成为朋友之后，两人开始了一场非常激烈的通信往来，关系很友好，但字面意义上永远在意见相左。所以他们之间有一场非常活跃的经济学辩论。而其中最核心的争论点是：爱尔兰完全专业化地只种土豆，到底行不行。历史学家对这些信件有多种解读，我觉得很难确切知道她的目的是什么。但基本上，玛丽亚写信给李嘉图说：我认为我们应该彻底专业化于土豆。我觉得爱尔兰就该全押在土豆上，其他一切都靠贸易换来。

turns.en: This is classic comparative advantage. If you can grow potatoes well, then that's what you should do.
turns.zh: 这就是经典的比较优势（comparative advantage）。如果你擅长种土豆，那你就该去种土豆。

turns.en: This is comparative advantage. She is literally parroting Ricardo's own idea back to him. She's saying, you know, like I buy it. Like comparative advantage works. We should just go all in on the potato. I think it's possible she's playing devil's advocate here. And it works if that's what she's doing because he comes back to her and says, ah, not sure about that. Like, I think it may actually be risky to so totally specialize in the potato. The potato is prone to failure. It's not worth you know, the profitability that comes with that kind of specialization if it leaves you capable of starving a nation, essentially. And so Ricardo complicates his own idea in a way that he really never does in his actual written texts. And in a way that he certainly never does in his arguments with Maltus. Like this, he basically argues what Maltus has been arguing to him for years in his letters to Mariah Edgeworth, which is fascinating from a historical perspective because it seems like he's complicating his own ideas. Very sadly, he then gets an ear infection and dies. And so he never, we never actually get this from Ricardo in any of his academic texts. It does not become part of his sort of, you know, legacy. Like he has a very simplistic view on trade. And that is what sort of becomes part of the canon. But we know that he complicated that because he did in these letters.
turns.zh: 这就是比较优势。她其实是在把李嘉图自己的观念原封不动地复述给他听。她在说：你懂的，我信这一套。比较优势是成立的，我们就该全押在土豆上。我觉得她有可能是在这里唱反调、故意抬杠，而且如果真是这样，那她成功了，因为李嘉图回信说：啊，这个我可不太确定。我觉得如此彻底地专业化于土豆，可能确实有风险。土豆容易歉收。如果这种专业化最终可能让一个国家挨饿，那它带来的利润就不值得。于是李嘉图把自己的观念复杂化了，而这是他在正式著述中从来没有做过的，也绝对没有在他与马尔萨斯的论战中做过。基本上，他在给玛丽亚·埃奇沃思的信里，反过来论证了马尔萨斯多年来一直对他论证的那个观点，这从历史角度看非常迷人，因为他似乎是在把自己的观念复杂化。很悲惨的是，他后来得了耳部感染去世了。所以我们从来没有在他任何学术文本中看到这一点，它也没有成为他遗产的一部分。他对贸易的看法非常简化，而那才是进入经典正典（canon）的东西。但我们知道他把这个看法复杂化过，因为他在这些书信里确实这么做了。

turns.en: But he was also right when it came to potatoes because Ireland then had a very famous potato famine.
turns.zh: 但在土豆这件事上他也是对的，因为爱尔兰后来发生了非常著名的大饥荒（potato famine）。

turns.en: Tragically, right?
turns.zh: 很悲剧，对吧？

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Yeah. And I think that this is actually a really interesting moment in Maria's development as an economist because it's very clear. Like I said, she may have been playing devil's advocate to some degree in these letters, but it is very clear from her writings that she is a devoted free trader up until the potato famine. She is very devoted to laissez-faire economics. She does not believe in any kind of handouts to the poor. Like she has taken the word of Adam Smith and she has interpreted it very literally. And she thinks that it should be applied pretty absolutely for much of her life. She then gets to the potato famine and everybody in her neighborhood is dying. It's like a huge tragedy. It hits her part of the country hard. It hits the whole country hard, but including her part of the country. And so she really sort of starts to revise her views, including with the sort of potato famine that predated the one we all know about. So there are two potato famines that hit in succession. The first one starts to complicate our views. The real one that we know about really, really complicates our views. She starts to come around to the idea that you might need to do some kind of government spending in times of extreme crisis, that you might have to just do handouts to get the economy back in action. She sort of comes around to an early version of what we would today call Keynesianism. Keynesianism obviously won't be developed for another 80 years.
turns.zh: 是的。而且我觉得这其实是玛丽亚作为经济学家成长过程中一个非常有意思的时刻，因为很清楚——就像我说的，她在这些信里可能在一定程度上是故意抬杠，但从她的著作中可以非常清楚地看到，直到土豆大饥荒之前，她都是一个坚定的自由贸易派。她非常信奉自由放任（laissez-faire）经济学，不相信任何形式对穷人的救济。她就是照着亚当·斯密的话去做，而且理解得非常字面化，认为在人生的大部分时间里都应该相当绝对地应用它。然后她遇上了土豆大饥荒，她所在社区里的人都在死去。这是一场巨大的悲剧，重创了她所在的地区，也重创了整个国家，包括她那一带。所以她真的开始修正自己的观点，包括在那场早于我们所熟知的大饥荒的土豆饥荒期间——当时接连发生了两次土豆饥荒。第一次开始让她的观念变得复杂，而我们都知道的那次真正的饥荒，则极大地复杂化了她的观念。她开始接受这样一个想法：在极端危机时期，你可能需要某种政府支出，你可能不得不直接发放救济，才能让经济重新运转起来。她有点转向了我们今天所说的凯恩斯主义（Keynesianism）的早期版本。当然，凯恩斯主义还要再过80年才会被提出。

turns.en: Until Keynes.
turns.zh: 直到凯恩斯出现。

turns.en: But yes. And so she really does change her views during the potato famine. And I think she, in particular, reflects on this conversation with Ricardo and thinks that she was wrong. In a very interesting turn of events, when she is dying, she actually, you know, people ask her, you know, you were so famous. You were the most famous author in the English language for a time. Do you want to write an autobiography? And she's like, no, but I would like to dictate some projects I didn't get to. And the first project she dictates basically is that somebody should think about the potato as a national food for Ireland. And she suggests that people look at David Ricardo's letters to her as a starting point.
turns.zh: 但是的。所以她确实在土豆大饥荒期间改变了自己的观点。而且我觉得她尤其反思了她与李嘉图的这场对话，认为自己错了。有一个非常有意思的转折：在她临终时，有人问她——你知道，你曾经那么有名，你有一段时间是英语世界最著名的作家——你想不想写一本自传？她说不想，但我想口述一些我没能完成的项目。而她口述的第一个项目，基本上就是应该有人把土豆当作爱尔兰的国民食物来研究。她建议人们把大卫·李嘉图写给她的信作为起点来看。

turns.en: Can you explain like, what was it about her story? Why was she so popular? Like, what was it about them in general?
turns.zh: 你能解释一下吗，她的故事到底有什么特别之处？她为什么那么受欢迎？总体来说，那些作品吸引人在哪儿？

turns.en: Yeah, because again, if you read The Cherry Orchard, to be completely honest, I know it's for kids in the early 1800s, but not that impressed, not that compelling.
turns.zh: 是啊，因为再说一次，如果你读《樱桃园》——说实话，我知道那是写给19世纪初的孩子看的——但真的没那么打动我，没那么引人入胜。

turns.en: So some of her children's literature, The Cherry Orchard, I will agree with you, not a joy to read. Some of her children's literature is more engaging and people found it very fun. Actually, Queen Victoria, when she was a child, used to try and write in the style of Maria Edgeworth because she thought she was so much fun. So yeah, so they were quite popular at the time with kids, which is interesting. The adult literature, I will say, is very funny. So Ennui is a good example of this. She has a sort of dry, cutting humor. She's very witty. And so that really shines through in her literature. And her characters are... caricatures of real people. And so it kind of does, it does work, I think, even today in Anhui's case. And at the time, it is just seen as wildly entertaining. And so she's very popular because these books are fun. She's also popular because people do want to learn these ideas at the time. I think it's worth noting that, so she obviously is putting these in pure fiction. She has mentors and is very good friends with a woman named Jane Marseille, who then sort of takes the idea of putting this stuff into fiction and takes it one step further and kind of puts it in what I think you can consider an early economics textbook. It is framed as a conversation between three women, but it is basically, for all intents and purposes, a textbook. It's an absolute bestseller. Like, it is a runaway hit. And so I think that, you know, what people are choosing to read at this time is a little bit different than what we think of as the bestseller list today. People were really curious about this stuff. And I think it's also worth noting what they've got to read at the time is The Wealth of Nations, which I don't know if you've ever read The Wealth of Nations, but it is not.
turns.zh: 她的部分儿童文学——《樱桃园》我同意你的看法，读起来不是一种享受。但她有些儿童文学作品更有吸引力，人们觉得非常有趣。事实上，维多利亚女王（Queen Victoria）小时候还曾试着模仿玛丽亚·埃奇沃思的风格来写作，因为她觉得她太有意思了。所以是的，她当时在儿童中相当受欢迎，这挺有意思的。至于成人文学，我得说，非常风趣。《Ennui》就是一个好例子。她有一种冷面、犀利的幽默感，非常机智，而这在她的文学作品里体现得淋漓尽致。她的人物原型都是……真实人物的漫画式写照。所以我觉得，即便放到今天，《Ennui》也是站得住的。而在当时，它就被视为极其有趣、极其好看。所以她受欢迎，是因为这些书有趣。她受欢迎也因为当时的人们确实想学这些观念。我觉得值得一提：她显然是把这些放在纯粹的虚构作品里，而她有一位导师，也是一位很好的朋友，名叫简·马塞特（Jane Marcet）。马塞特后来把“把这些东西写进虚构作品”的思路又推进了一步，写成了一本我认为可以算作早期经济学教科书的东西。它被设定为三位女性之间的对话，但从各方面看，它其实就是一本教科书。它是绝对的畅销书，是现象级的大热。所以我觉得，那个时代人们选择读的东西，和我们今天理解的畅销书排行榜有点不一样。人们真的对这些东西很好奇。而且我觉得还值得一提：他们当时能读的是《国富论》，我不知道你有没有读过《国富论》，但它并不

turns.en: A joy to read.
turns.zh: ——是一本好读的书。

turns.en: It's very, very dense. Yeah, it's very dense. It's difficult to understand what he's saying sometimes. And at the time, when these ideas are all new, it's really difficult. Like people don't understand it. And so I think the ability to read these books, get a better sort of analogy, of what the Wealth of Nations is trying to say, and then to be able to talk about the Wealth of Nations in an informed way is actually really attractive.
turns.zh: 它非常非常艰深。是的，非常艰深。有时候很难理解他在说什么。而在当时，这些观念全都是新的，那就更难了，人们根本读不懂。所以我觉得，能够读这些书、对《国富论》想说什么得到一个更好的类比理解，然后能够有见地地谈论《国富论》，这件事其实非常有吸引力。

turns.en: You also write about, she had an important disagreement with Smith on one thing. So she agreed about the free trade aspect and But she disagreed about the value of labor. So I guess Smith had this idea that unless you're producing something like a potato or, I don't know, a factory component or something like that, it didn't really have value. Whereas Maria argued that people who are producing other things like, I don't know, lawyers or accountants, those are ephemeral, non-physical things, but because they're making people's lives better. Maybe not in the case of lawyers. Because they're making people's lives better, that that still has some value. Can you talk to us about that disagreement and how that kind of played out in the future of economics?
turns.zh: 你还写到，她在有一件事上和斯密有重要分歧。她在自由贸易这一点上是同意的，但在劳动的价值上不同意。我想斯密的观点是，除非你生产的是像土豆这样的东西，或者，我不知道，某个工厂零部件之类的，否则就谈不上真正的价值。而玛丽亚则认为，那些生产其他东西的人，比如——我不知道——律师或会计师，那些是短暂的、非实体的东西，但因为他们让人们的生活变得更好（律师可能不算），因为他们让人们的生活变得更好，所以那依然具有某种价值。你能跟我们谈谈这个分歧，以及它在经济学后来的发展中是如何展开的吗？

turns.en: Yeah. So she was early to an idea that we basically still think is right today, which is that Utility is kind of the basis of value as opposed to labor. So Smith is labor theory of value. This is somewhat complicated. He is not actually as clear on his theory of value as I think some historians make him out to be. And I think there's a reassessment going on about what he thought about the basis of value. But certainly the classical economists in general, Ricardo Maltese, think that labor is the basis of value. And She comes in and she really questions that. And she questions it in a very subtle way in her literature. She, the character who sort of like wins in Castle Rackrent, who takes over, is trained as a lawyer. And so, you know, I think she's basically saying, you know, you can have, in this new economy, in this new world we're forming, you can have productive people.
turns.zh: 是的。她很早就提出了一个我们今天基本上仍认为正确的观念，那就是：价值的基础是效用（utility），而不是劳动。斯密讲的是劳动价值论（labor theory of value）。这件事有点复杂。他在价值理论上其实并不像某些历史学家所描绘的那样清晰，而且我认为关于他对价值基础的看法，目前正在有一场重新评估。但可以肯定的是，古典经济学家整体上——李嘉图、马尔萨斯——都认为劳动是价值的基础。而她站出来，真的对这一点提出了质疑。而且她在文学作品里用非常微妙的方式提出质疑：在《拉克伦特城堡》里，那个可以说是最终胜出、接手一切的角色，受的是律师训练。所以我觉得她基本上是在说，在这个新经济体里、在我们正在形成的这个新世界里，是可以存在有生产力的人的。

turns.en: Physical labor is not the be all and end all of the economy.
turns.zh: 体力劳动并不是经济的全部和终极。

turns.en: Exactly. And so she's coming in and saying, like, something has changed here and we should reconsider it. It's very subtle there. It's much less subtle in some of her correspondence and in particular, her father's correspondence. It's pretty clear from her father's correspondence that Maria and her father are thinking about utility as a basis for value and think that Smith is wrong about this. He at one point in time says in a letter to one of the Benthamites, you know, I think we could correct some errors in Adam Smith's thinking with this concept. And so She's very much early to this train. And I think that, you know, in a way that ends up becoming influential and really sort of the way that we think about value now.
turns.zh: 正是。所以她是在说：这里有些东西变了，我们应该重新考虑。在小说里这一点非常微妙。但在她的一些通信里，尤其是她父亲的通信里，就远没那么微妙了。从她父亲的书信中可以很清楚地看到，玛丽亚和她父亲都在把效用当作价值的基础来思考，并且认为斯密在这一点上是错的。她父亲有一次在写给一位边沁主义者的信中说：我觉得我们可以用这个概念纠正亚当·斯密思想中的一些错误。所以她非常早地踏上了这趟列车，而且我认为，是以一种最终产生了影响力、并真的塑造了我们今天思考价值的方式。

turns.en: So So when we think about the transition of economics from its early political economy days, where you have Adam Smith writing these kind of dense treatises, treatise, treatise? I never know how to- Treatises. Treatises, thank you, about economics. And then you have someone like Maria, who's trying to illustrate them in a sort of practical behavioral economics manner. And then you have the evolution into abstract models of Are we at a moment in time where people are kind of, it feels like people are still trying to meld those two worlds together and we constantly get the swing from practical behavioral economics back into theory. And then, I don't know, it feels like it's just the pendulum swinging back and forth constantly.
turns.zh: 那么，当我们思考经济学从早期政治经济学时代的转型——那时亚当·斯密写的是那种很艰深的论著，treatise？treatises？我永远搞不清怎么念——论著（treatises），谢谢——关于经济学的论著。然后你有像玛丽亚这样的人，试图用一种实用的、行为经济学式的方式来阐释它们。再到后来演变成抽象模型。我们现在是不是正处在一个时刻，人们还在试图把这两个世界融合起来，我们不断看到从实用的行为经济学摆回理论，然后又——我不知道——感觉就像钟摆在不停来回摆动。

turns.en: Yeah, I do think the pendulum is swinging back and forth constantly. I do think that one thing that is particularly interesting, you know, as somebody who's covered these issues for a long time and that I thought about a lot while I was writing the book, is that one lesson from this era is that people who were applying economics in a really absolute way often ended up finding that to be problematic. And by, you know, with the benefit of time. And I think I've also seen that play out in my own career and my own observation of modern economics. You know, I think there are rules in economics. They are not like physics. And I think that every few years we have a reappraisal where we have some model that was supposed to work absolutely and has started to break down. And, you know, everyone is reassessing.
turns.zh: 是的，我确实认为钟摆在不停地来回摆动。我确实认为有一点特别有意思——作为一个长期报道这些议题的人，也是我在写这本书时反复思考的——那就是：这个时代给我们的一个教训是，那些以绝对化方式应用经济学的人，往往最后会发现这样做是有问题的。当然，这是事后回看才清楚的。而且我觉得在我自己的职业生涯中、在我自己对现代经济学的观察中，也看到过同样的情形上演。你知道，我认为经济学里是有规律的，但它们不像物理学那样。我觉得每隔几年我们都会有一次重新评估：某个本该绝对奏效的模型开始失灵了，然后所有人都在重新审视。

turns.en: Crops fail or people make the wrong decision or people get greedy. And that deviates from the model. Yeah.
turns.zh: 作物歉收，或者人们做了错误的决定，或者人们变得贪婪。于是现实就偏离了模型。是的。

turns.en: Or we misunderstand some variable in the model and how it will affect everything. And so, you know, I do think that, you know, we can get a little bit overly DSGE reliant. And I think that there's something to be said for, you know, remembering that this is a philosophy at its root and it's not physics. And so, you know, I think there are some interesting applications to today.
turns.zh: 或者我们误解了模型中的某个变量，误解了它会如何影响其他一切。所以你知道，我确实认为，我们可能会有点过度依赖 DSGE 模型（动态随机一般均衡模型）。而且我认为，记住这门学问根源上是一种哲学、而不是物理学，这一点是有道理的。所以我觉得这里面有一些对今天很有意思的启示。

turns.en: Do you miss the Fedbeat?
turns.zh: 你会想念跑美联储这条线吗？

turns.en: Oh, of course I miss the Fed beat. The Fed beat was a fun beat. I mean, geopolitics is fun too. So it's not like I'm doing something boring now.
turns.zh: 哦，当然想念。美联储这条线很有意思。我是说，地缘政治也挺有意思的，所以并不是说我现在在做无聊的事。

turns.en: How much overlap is there between European parliamentary politics and the Fed beat? What's the connective tissue there?
turns.zh: 欧洲议会政治和美联储报道之间有多少重叠？两者的连接点在哪里？

turns.en: There is a lot of overlap between the European Commission, which is sort of the beating heart of the regulatory and trade state in European Union politics, and Fed reporting, because it is similarly trying to make policy for a constituency of 27. And so there are lots of little fiefdoms and there are lots of coalitions and lots of people who need to be satisfied. And it feels quite similar to the Fed with its 12 districts where you've got various people who are going to sort of weigh in on the issue and who you have to satisfy with one central decision.
turns.zh: 欧盟委员会（European Commission）——它算是欧盟政治中监管与贸易体系跳动的心脏——和美联储报道之间有很多重叠，因为它同样是在为一个由27个成员组成的群体制定政策。所以那里有很多小小的“封地”，有很多联盟，有很多需要被安抚的人。这和美联储及其12个联邦储备区感觉很相似：各色人等都会对某个议题发表意见，而你必须用一个中央决策让所有人都满意。

turns.en: It's interesting because in some sense, macro is super interesting right now. Inflation is still elevated, highly uncertain. On the other hand, and I think we all, Tracy and I feel it, a lot of people feel it, the big questions of the day do not feel cyclical. It's like these big structural questions. What is the long-term future of Europe as a coherent block? What is the long-term future of the US-China relationship? What is the long-term future of how AI will change the economy? And so on some level, Even though it is very interesting to still listen to the press conferences and watch the CPI, the jobs report and all that, it does feel like some of that stuff is just being overtaken by stuff that these month-to-month things just don't matter to people the same way they used to.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，从某种意义上说，宏观现在超级有意思。通胀仍然偏高，且高度不确定。但另一方面——我觉得我们所有人，崔西和我都有这种感觉，很多人都有——当今的重大问题感觉并不是周期性的，而是这些大的结构性问题：欧洲作为一个有凝聚力的集团，长期前景是什么？中美关系的长期前景是什么？AI 将如何改变经济，长期前景是什么？所以在某个层面上，尽管听那些新闻发布会、盯 CPI、就业报告等等仍然很有意思，但确实感觉其中一些东西正在被另一些东西盖过——这些逐月的数据对人们来说，已经不像过去那样重要了。

turns.en: Completely. And not to literally talk my own book here, but I feel like it does feel kind of like the early 1800s right now. You know, it's like it feels a little bit like the dawn of the Industrial Revolution.
turns.zh: 完全同意。不是为了字面意义上地“推销自己的书”（talk my own book），但我真觉得现在有点像19世纪初。你知道，感觉有点像工业革命的黎明。

turns.en: I was just about to ask what an Edgeworthian interpretation of AI and the economy would be like. There must be parallels.
turns.zh: 我正想问，如果用埃奇沃思式的视角来解读 AI 与经济，会是什么样子。两者之间肯定有相似之处。

turns.en: Yeah, I think there definitely are because I think this moment feels so much like basically 1800. Say more about that.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得肯定有，因为我认为当下这个时刻实在太像——基本上就是1800年。“那你多说说这个。”

turns.en: Basically 1800.
turns.zh: 基本上就是1800年？

turns.en: Yeah. It's the very dawn of the industrial revolution. You can see it coming. The division of labor is starting to be applied. Factories are becoming a lot more efficient. London is kind of industrializing and everything is changing. Agriculture has just recently become significantly more efficient. The economy is just in a state of absolute flux. And it seems very clear that there are going to be a lot of people who were previously farmers or sharecroppers or sort of just traveling around doing sort of menial jobs who are going to be disenfranchised by this or who are going to have their lives fundamentally change. There's a lot of concern that factories are going to turn people into robots because they're just going to be doing repetitive tasks without having to apply any real critical thinking to them. And at the same time, we're seeing huge political ruptures. You know, it's the wake of the French Revolution. Everybody is afraid that there are going to be uprisings elsewhere. There are, in fact, uprisings elsewhere, including in Ireland in 1798. And so there's a huge sort of political sort of populist wave that is playing out. Then there's the backlash to that populist wave. And it's colliding with a bunch of economic forces that are fundamentally changing everything. And this is really how we get modern economics. It's because the world is trying to find a new way to explain itself, essentially. Everything has changed and we need to understand it. And so I feel like that has a lot of parallels to today, right? Like we can see that AI is happening. We can see that it's going to change everything. It's not, I mean, we can quibble about the numbers, but I think we can probably agree that it's not fundamentally changing everything yet. Like you see it in the data, but it has not caused some sort of like seismic wave yet. But it seems likely, and many people think that it's coming. It's clearly changing the way economic actors relate to each other. And it's coming at the same time that we're seeing these populous waves across Europe, but also obviously here in the U.S. And we are also seeing this sort of reshuffling of the global order as China becomes becomes whatever China is now becoming. And as the rest of the world tries to react to that, and as the rest of the world reacts to the shift in American trade policy. And so huge moment of flux, really kind of challenging, I think, the way we understand the modern economy. And so in that way, I think there's a real parallel.
turns.zh: 是的。那正是工业革命的破晓时分。你能看到它正在到来。分工开始被应用，工厂的效率大幅提高，伦敦正在工业化，一切都在改变。农业刚刚变得显著更高效，经济处于彻底的流动状态。而且很明显，将会有很多人——此前是农民、佃农，或者只是四处打零工做粗活的人——会因为这场变化而被剥夺权益，或者他们的人生会被彻底改变。当时有很多人担心，工厂会把人变成机器人，因为他们只是在做重复性的工作，不需要运用任何真正的批判性思考。与此同时，我们还看到巨大的政治断裂。那是法国大革命的余波，所有人都害怕其他地方会爆发起义。事实上其他地方确实爆发了起义，包括1798年的爱尔兰。所以有一股巨大的民粹主义政治浪潮正在展开，然后是对这股民粹浪潮的反弹。而这一切又与一堆正在从根本上改变一切的经济力量相撞。这其实就是现代经济学的由来：世界在试图找到一种新的方式解释自己。一切都变了，我们需要理解它。所以我觉得这和今天有很多相似之处，对吧？我们能看到 AI 正在发生，能看到它将改变一切。它还没有——我是说，具体数字我们可以争论，但我想我们大概能同意，它还没有从根本上改变一切。你在数据里能看到它，但它还没有引发某种地震级的冲击波。但这似乎很可能发生，很多人认为它正在到来。它显然正在改变经济主体之间相互关联的方式。而它到来的同时，我们正看到席卷欧洲的民粹浪潮，当然在美国也一样。我们也看到全球秩序的重新洗牌：中国正在变成中国如今正在变成的样子，世界其他地方在试图对此作出反应，也在对美国贸易政策的转变作出反应。所以这是一个巨大的流动时刻，我认为它真的在挑战我们理解现代经济的方式。从这个意义上说，我觉得确实存在真正的相似之处。

turns.en: But this was also, and I'm just parroting your own book back to you, but this was Maria's reason for writing about economics in the way that she did, right? Her argument was that in a time of economic flux, one of the things you can do to empower displaced people and workers is educate them about how all of this stuff is supposed to work or could work.
turns.zh: 但这也是——我只是在把你自己的书复述给你听——这也是玛丽亚以那种方式写经济学的原因，对吧？她的论点是：在经济剧烈变动的时期，你能做的事情之一，就是让被取代的人和工人获得力量，办法是教育他们，让他们明白这一切本该如何运作、或者可以如何运作。

turns.en: Yeah, and I think basically what she was hoping to do is give people the tools for flexibility, essentially. I think she thought that if you were educated and if you were capable of sort of understanding the world around you, you had the ability to have some kind of economic mobility. And so I think there are some interesting parallels to that today. You know, I think a lot of our companies are probably pushing us to learn as much about artificial intelligence as we can in the hope that we can understand how to apply it as whatever comes down the pipeline comes down the pipeline. I feel like that feels like a somewhat similar moment.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得她基本上希望做的，就是给人们提供灵活应变的工具。我认为她觉得，如果你受过教育、如果你有能力理解周围的世界，你就有可能实现某种程度的经济流动。所以我觉得这在今天有一些很有意思的对应。你知道，我想我们很多公司大概都在推动我们尽可能多地学习人工智能，希望我们能理解如何应用它，无论接下来流水线上出来的是什么。我觉得那是一个颇为相似的时刻。

turns.en: Yeah. All right, Gina, thank you so much for coming back on All Thoughts. The book, again, is The Invisible Hand of Maria Edgeworth. Thanks so much. Thank you for having me. Joe, I love that conversation.
turns.zh: 好。吉安娜，非常感谢你再次来到《Odd Lots》。这本书再提一次，是《玛丽亚·埃奇沃思的看不见的手》。太感谢了。“谢谢你们邀请我。”乔，我太喜欢这段对话了。

turns.en: Yeah, me too.
turns.zh: 是的，我也是。

turns.en: It's such an interesting aspect of economic history that, again, I had never heard of before today. It's kind of depressing that we have an influential female economist who was working and was popular at the dawn of political economy as a sort of academic subject. And her legacy was basically completely erased.
turns.zh: 这是经济史中如此有意思的一面，而再说一次，我今天之前从未听说过。有点令人沮丧的是：在政治经济学作为一门学科破晓之时，有一位有影响力的女性经济学家既在工作又很受欢迎，而她的遗产却基本上被彻底抹去了。

turns.en: It's fascinating how that can happen. That she wasn't just sort of influential within economics. She was popular among people, among readers. The fact that someone can be like, oh, in their day, they outsold Jane Austen. And then it's like literally no one has heard of this person.
turns.zh: 这种事竟然会发生，真是令人惊叹。她不只是在经济学内部有影响力，她在普通大众中、在读者中都很受欢迎。一个人可以说“在他们那个年代，他们的书卖得比简·奥斯汀还好”，然后却变成了字面意义上没人听说过这个人。

turns.en: And you can't blame it completely on. Shifts in literary taste because there are plenty of important historical authors who you go back and read now and they're terrible and you're like what is this stuff yeah one question i want to ask you you know we were talking about children's books and children's stories are children's books nowadays still really moralistic they're a lot.
turns.zh: 而且你不能把这完全归咎于文学品味的变迁，因为有很多重要的历史作家，你现在回头去读，会觉得糟透了，心里想这写的都是什么东西。是的。我还想问你一个问题：我们刚才在聊儿童读物和儿童故事——如今的儿童读物是不是还那么道德说教味十足？那可真够受的。

turns.en: Yeah they're a lot it's a real it's a real mix some aren't some are just like sort of normal there's definitely a lot of like Yeah, moralistic children's books.
turns.zh: 是啊，那可真够受的。真的是五花八门，有些不是，有些就很正常，但确实有很多那种——嗯，道德说教味很重的儿童读物。

turns.en: When I was reading about the cherry orchard, I remembered a book that my mom gave to me, my Austrian mother. And I don't know if anyone in America would have heard of it. It's called like, slovenly peter or something in english.
turns.zh: 我在读关于《樱桃园》的内容时，想起了一本书，是我妈妈——我那位奥地利母亲——给我的。我不知道美国有没有人听说过它。它在英文里好像叫《邋遢彼得》（Slovenly Peter）之类的。

turns.en: Have you ever heard of this book it's.
turns.zh: 你们听说过这本书吗？它——

turns.en: Absolutely terrifying it's an old book from i want to say like 1800s in german and it's all it's like tales of children dying from doing stupid things like lighting themselves on fire but it's illustrated oh wow No one look it up unless you want nightmares. To be disturbed. But I think I would have preferred reading a book about the division of labor as a child versus don't set yourself on fire.
turns.zh: ——简直是恐怖至极。这是本老书，我想大概是19世纪的，德文的，全都是讲小孩子因为做蠢事而死掉的故事，比如把自己点着。而且是配插图的。“哇哦。”千万别去查，除非你想做噩梦、想被吓到。不过我觉得，比起“别把自己点着”，我小时候宁愿读一本讲分工的书。

turns.en: That's so funny.
turns.zh: 太好笑了。
